result:
The city was doing what cities always do at twilight: collecting itself. Windows blinked on one by one, neon signs warmed into brightness, and the wind carried small promises between buildings. I walked without any particular destination, which is a luxury I rarely allow myself, as if aimlessness could be a kind of medicine.

Along the river, the water moved like a sheet being pulled gently across a table. Reflections trembled—streetlights turned into wavering coins, clouds became bruised fingerprints on the surface, and the moon looked less like a presence than an idea. Every now and then I heard laughter from somewhere I couldn’t see, and it made me think of how many lives overlap without ever meeting.

A bus sighed at the curb and exhaled people into the evening. A cyclist cut through the corner of my vision, disappearing as quickly as they arrived, their silence threaded with the soft rhythm of tires. I watched a window above a bakery. For a moment the lights were steady, and then—like a curtain being lifted—the glass caught a flash of flour and someone inside began to work.

It occurred to me that the world runs on small repetitions. Kneading dough. Stirring coffee. Turning keys. The grandest changes happen by degrees, the way dusk becomes night without a single dramatic moment to announce it.

When I finally stopped walking, I realized I had been moving all along—away from noise, toward something calmer.
